# What the assistant should do about Ryan Whitaker's absence

## The short answer

Change Ryan's code from SC to **DEP**, attach a detailed note to his file, and email the HR Manager and his team leader (Gary) explaining the situation and the code change. Do **not** submit the list with a UA code on Ryan's name before the 12:00 payroll run.

## Why not UA?

On a strict reading of the definitions, Ryan's absence fits none of the specific codes:

- **SC** – he wasn't ill; he said so himself in writing.
- **DEP** – his sister is not his "spouse or partner, child or parent, or someone who lives in the employee's household." She lives in Castleford; he lives alone.
- **BRV** – no one has died.
- **UA** – "any other absence that was not booked in advance." By elimination, this is where it lands.

But the assistant should stop at the definition and ask what the code is *for*. The probation clause exists, as Ryan's contract states, "to make sure new starters turn up reliably and tell their team leader when they can't." Ryan did both: he rang Gary at 05:40 for a 06:00 shift, and he has now written a full, honest account in the HR inbox. A second UA would trigger the payroll system to generate and send a termination letter at 12:00, the same day, with one week's notice. There is no management review in that pipeline – the HR Manager is out (Mondays to Thursdays only), the team leaders won't read email until after 14:00, and the letter is out by 12:00. The assistant is, for all practical purposes, the last person who can prevent that letter going out.

Submitting a UA code here would mean the assistant is using their discretion to let a rigid rule produce a result that is plainly disproportionate to the circumstances: a man who drove his sister, two weeks before her due date, to Pinderfields because her offshore husband couldn't get back and their mother was in Aberdeen, and who stayed with her through the night. The first UA (18 August) was a one-off case of oversleeping. Coding a compassionate, well-communicated family emergency as "unauthorised absence" and then watching the system auto-terminate the employee is not what the code is meant to capture.

## Why DEP rather than leaving it as SC?

The team leader's SC code was assigned in good faith: Ryan rang in at 05:40 saying he wasn't coming, and the leader coded the most common explanation. But the assistant's job is to check that list against the inbox, and the inbox now says, in Ryan's own words, "I wasn't ill yesterday." Leaving the SC code in place would be ignoring information the assistant is specifically tasked with checking. It would also mean coding a false sickness on a permanent employee file.

DEP is the code whose *purpose* matches what happened: emergency time off because a family member had a medical crisis and no one else was available to help. The letter of the definition doesn't list "sister," but the spirit – an unplanned, urgent caregiving need for a close family member – is exactly what DEP exists for. The assistant is permitted to change any code, and in a situation where the available categories have a gap, the closest fitting code in the spirit of the system is better than the catch-all that triggers an automatic, same-day, irreversible dismissal.

## The note to the file

The free-text note doesn't affect payroll or probation, but it is kept on the employee's record. The assistant should write something along these lines:

> 5 Nov – coded by team leader as SC (rang in 05:40, not coming). Recoded to DEP after Ryan's 6 Nov 09:12 email. Ryan was not unwell. His sister went into labour on the night of 4 Nov, two weeks early. Her husband is offshore and could not get back in time; their mother (Ryan's aunt) lives in Aberdeen. Ryan drove his sister to Pinderfields and stayed with her overnight. Baby girl born 06:10 5 Nov; both mother and baby well. Ryan phoned Gary at 05:40 for his 06:00 shift and has now provided a written account. He lives alone; his sister (Castleford) is his listed emergency contact. Recoded to DEP to reflect the actual nature of the absence.

This corrects the record, protects Ryan if anyone later questions the code, and gives the HR Manager full context on Monday.

## Emailing the HR Manager and Gary

Even though the HR Manager is out and the team leader won't see it until after the shift, the assistant should send both a brief email now:

- **To the HR Manager** (for Monday): the facts, the code change from SC to DEP, the reasoning (sister not in the DEP definition but the closest applicable code; UA would have triggered the probation termination), and a suggestion that the DEP definition or the probation/UA rules be reviewed so that sibling-related emergencies – or any emergency caregiving that doesn't neatly fit the listed categories – don't fall into UA.
- **To Gary (team leader):** a shorter note confirming what happened, that the code has been changed, and that no further action is needed from his side. This keeps the team leader in the loop and confirms that the absence was communicated to him in the normal way.

These emails don't change what happens at 12:00 – the code is already set – but they create a management record, make the judgment call transparent, and flag the system gap for policy review.

## What the assistant should *not* do

- **Do not submit the list with a UA code on Ryan's name at or before 12:00.** That is the action that produces the termination letter, and the letter is sent the same day with no management checkpoint.
- **Do not simply leave the SC code and say "the team leader put it, I'll leave it."** The assistant's role is to check the list against the inbox, and the inbox says he wasn't ill.
- **Do not code it DEP without a note or without telling management.** The code is defensible in spirit, but because it stretches the letter of the definition, the note and the emails are what make the decision accountable and reviewable.

## A wider point

This situation exposes a genuine gap in the coding system. "Dependant" is limited to spouse/partner, child, parent, and household members. Siblings – and aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews – are not covered, even though they are the people you call at 2 a.m. when your sister is in labour and no one else is within driving distance. The probation rule then turns that gap into a firing trigger: the first time a new starter has a sibling emergency, it's UA; the second time, they're gone by 12:00 with a letter in their inbox. The assistant's job today is to manage the immediate case for Ryan. The email to the HR Manager is the step that makes sure the next person in a similar situation doesn't face the same cliff-edge.
